title: TranscriptFormer: A generative cell atlas across 1.5 billion years of evolution.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Paper has no open full text or supplement in Europe PMC (no PMCID). I fetched the GitHub README (czi-ai/transcriptformer): weights are downloadable from AWS S3 with no login; the README recommends a GPU (A100 40GB) for running the model. I fetched the CELLxGENE Census release notes, which list precomputed cell embeddings 'tf-sapiens', 'tf-exemplar-human' and 'tf-exemplar-mouse', plus the number of distinct cell-type labels: 898 human, 473 mouse, 40 marmoset, 54 macaque, 25 chimpanzee.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: 112 million training cells across 12 species, the state-of-the-art cross-species cell-type claims, and the zero-shot disease results come from the abstract and README only. I did not open any Census cell table or embedding array: cellxgene_census and tiledbsoma (the libraries that read Census) are not installed, and I followed the no-install rule. A blog/tweet says the embeddings cover 106M human and 42M mouse cells; I did not verify that.

a1_downloadable.note: Census is a public S3-hosted store with no login, and model weights are public on S3. Checked from documentation; no file actually downloaded.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Cell type, disease, tissue and species are standard Census metadata columns (the release notes count distinct values per column). Seen in the docs, not in a downloaded table.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs are count matrices and precomputed TranscriptFormer embeddings stored in Census itself; no identifier lookups needed. Documentation only.

a4_units_stated.note: Raw UMI (unique molecular identifier) counts, and embeddings are unitless vectors; labels are categorical ontology terms. Not checked in files.

a5_enough_rows.note: Millions of cells per species according to Census, but I counted no rows myself. The real independent unit is the dataset/donor, likely hundreds per species for human and mouse.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~1-3 GB for a subsample of a few hundred thousand cells with 2,048-dim embeddings (estimate)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Running TranscriptFormer itself needs a GPU, but Census precomputed embeddings for human and mouse remove that need. Cross-species work beyond human and mouse would need GPU inference.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Not checked: no row counts opened. The Census release notes carry their own cell-type counts; I could not compare them with the paper.

a8_label_provenance.note: Cell-type labels are annotations submitted by each dataset's authors and mapped to the Cell Ontology. Some were themselves made with automated reference-mapping tools, which adds mild circularity and varies between datasets.

B1.why: Census obs table plus a separate embedding array, joined on soma_joinid; documented API, not opened by me.

B2.why: Needs the cellxgene_census/TileDB-SOMA libraries rather than plain csv; not tested here.

B3.why: Labels are mapped to a shared Cell Ontology, but granularity differs between datasets and annotating labs.

B4.why: Categorical labels, nothing censored; 'unknown' cell types are easy to drop.

B5.why: Census flags duplicate cells (is_primary_data column, per docs); easy to filter.

B6.why: Census schema documents every obs column publicly.

C1.why: A study of how human-to-mouse transfer degrades by tissue is informative either way, but VCBench already covers much of this.

C2.why: TranscriptFormer, UCE and SATURN are all open, and VCBench and a zero-shot benchmark (2026) have already evaluated them honestly.

C3.why: Weak angle: per-tissue calibration of cross-species transfer; benchmarks already exist.

C4.why: Manual cell-type annotation is slow, but automated reference mapping is already routine.

C5.why: Published baselines exist: scVI embeddings in Census, PCA plus logistic regression, VCBench linear baselines.

D1.why: TranscriptFormer weights are open, and its embeddings are precomputed in Census.

D2.why: Precomputed human/mouse embeddings allow fitting a head on CPU; new species would need a GPU.

D3.why: Licence of the weights not checked; Census data is mostly CC-BY. Treat it as unclear or non-commercial.

E1.why: Hold out whole datasets, donors, tissues or species; dataset_id is a Census column.

E2.why: Hundreds of datasets in human and mouse Census (per docs, not counted).

E3.why: Majority class per tissue, and scVI or PCA embeddings with the same classifier.

E4.why: No replicate annotations; disagreement between labs over labels could be estimated only roughly.

E5.why: Positive control: major lineages (T cell vs hepatocyte) must separate near-perfectly across species.

E6.why: Shuffle labels; swap in random or scVI embeddings.

E7.why: Primate datasets (macaque, marmoset, chimpanzee) in Census, never seen in training, serve as external validation.

E8.why: The repo notebook reproduces macaque-to-marmoset cell-type transfer; this would need GPU inference.

G1.why: Ensembl gene IDs and Cell Ontology IDs in Census (per schema docs).

G2.why: Plausible partners include the Bgee orthology/expression database and the Cell Ontology hierarchy.

G3.why: Orthology mapping between species is many-to-many for gene families.

G4.why: Linking transfer errors to evolutionary distance is a modest extension of what the paper already shows.

H1.why: Healthy vs disease cells exist in human; for cell types 'negatives' are not a meaningful concept.

H2.why: Human and mouse dominate; other species are thin (25-54 cell types each, per release notes).

H3.why: The claim can be stated precisely in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3).

H4.why: Species and tissue imbalance is visible in Census summaries; annotation provenance is less obvious.

I1.why: Single-cell atlas and comparative biology community; no specific decision-maker.

I2.why: Could guide which reference to use for annotation in a new species; marginal.

I3.why: Macro-F1 for cell types roughly matches the annotation task.

I4.why: VCBench reports that linear baselines match foundation models on cross-species transfer.

J1.why: Real modelling: grouped splits, frozen embeddings, transfer evaluation.

J2.why: Cell-type plausibility needs some single-cell domain knowledge.

J3.why: A benchmark table by tissue is shareable even if no gain is found.

existing_models.name: TranscriptFormer (TF-Metazoa/Exemplar/Sapiens), this paper
existing_models.score_and_split: Abstract claims state-of-the-art cross-species cell-type classification, including species 685 million years apart; exact numbers and splits not seen (no full text).

existing_models.name: UCE (Universal Cell Embeddings), Nature 2026
existing_models.score_and_split: Outperforms SATURN and SAMap on cell-type transfer from human to novel species for 3 of 4 datasets (per search summary).

existing_models.name: SATURN, Nature Methods 2024
existing_models.score_and_split: Supervised cross-species integration; numbers not retrieved.

existing_models.name: VCBench benchmark, bioRxiv 2026
existing_models.score_and_split: Linear baselines match or beat Geneformer, scGPT, UCE, TranscriptFormer and State on 4 of 5 dimensions, including cross-species transfer; TranscriptFormer wins RNA-to-protein prediction (+53% Pearson).

backbone.name: TranscriptFormer tf-exemplar (precomputed Census embeddings for human and mouse)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU for heads on precomputed embeddings; GPU needed for any species not in Census
backbone.licence: Not verified; Census data mostly CC-BY 4.0

integration.partner_dataset: Cell Ontology hierarchy plus Bgee/Ensembl Compara orthology
integration.join_key: Cell Ontology ID; Ensembl gene ID
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do errors in human-to-mouse cell-type transfer concentrate in cell types whose marker genes lack one-to-one orthologs?

controls.positive_control: Major lineages (immune vs epithelial vs neuronal) separate near-perfectly across species; marker genes rediscovered.
controls.negative_control: Shuffled labels; random or PCA embeddings of matched dimension.
controls.external_validation: Census primate datasets (macaque, marmoset, chimpanzee) not used to train TranscriptFormer.

honest_claim_h3: Among cells in public CELLxGENE human and mouse datasets, annotated by their submitting labs, a classifier on frozen TranscriptFormer embeddings transfers cell-type labels across species with tissue-dependent accuracy relative to simple baselines.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a pretrained cell model's summary of each mouse cell to predict its cell type from human training cells, and map where it fails.
plain_idea.train_on: Precomputed TranscriptFormer embeddings for human single cells from CELLxGENE Census, with author-assigned cell-type labels; number of cells unknown (not counted).
plain_idea.predict: The cell type of mouse (or primate) cells, checked against the labels the original study authors assigned, mapped onto the Cell Ontology.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Tells atlas builders which tissues and cell types can trust cross-species label transfer; but recent benchmarks already largely answer this.

more_or_better_data.why: We would use the same CELLxGENE corpus TranscriptFormer and UCE were trained and evaluated on; there is no new data.

confidence_score.why: Many datasets per cell type allow per-tissue calibration, but whether existing models already report it was not checked.

models_beatable.why: TranscriptFormer (2025/2026, ~1B-parameter transformer) and UCE (Nature 2026) are recent and open; VCBench (2026) has already done the honest baseline comparison.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No new joinable data that measures the same labels; the evaluation data is the training corpus.

label_elsewhere.sources: CELLxGENE Census itself, Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens and Tabula Muris (known resources)
label_elsewhere.why: Cell-type labels exist across many independent atlases, so held-out-atlas external validation is easy.

ambitious.why: Publishes single-cell benchmarks; would need a clear, new failure pattern in cross-species transfer tied to orthology.

realistic.why: Accepts focused benchmark and re-evaluation studies of existing tools.

fallback.journal: bioRxiv preprint plus an ML-for-biology workshop
fallback.why: A negative result (linear baselines match TranscriptFormer per tissue) fits a workshop note.

pitch.headline: Precomputed TranscriptFormer embeddings for human and mouse Census cells make a cross-species cell-model benchmark possible on a laptop, with no GPU.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: Census release notes list 898 human and 473 mouse cell types, plus primate data, all under one ontology; embeddings are precomputed (docs only, files not opened).
pitch.the_win: A per-tissue map showing where TranscriptFormer embeddings beat scVI or PCA for human-to-mouse label transfer, and by how much macro-F1 changes.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: Confirms VCBench's finding that linear baselines match foundation models, broken down by tissue; this adds little that is new.
pitch.who_wants_it: CZI Virtual Cells Platform and single-cell atlas annotators choosing a reference model for new species.

ml_idea: Fit logistic-regression or MLP heads on precomputed TranscriptFormer and scVI embeddings for human cells, test on mouse and held-out primate datasets with leave-dataset-out splits, and break transfer accuracy down by tissue and ortholog coverage.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, nothing timed: a subsample of ~300k cells × 2,048 float32 values is ~2.5 GB; logistic regression on CPU takes minutes.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Install cellxgene_census via uv, then confirm the tf-exemplar-mouse embedding loads for a 10k-cell subset and the per-dataset cell-type counts.

verdict_reason: This is a foundation-model paper, not a dataset: the data is the public CELLxGENE Census, and the cross-species cell-typing task is crowded. TranscriptFormer, UCE and SATURN are all open, and 2026 benchmarks (VCBench) already compared them honestly with linear baselines. Precomputed embeddings make a laptop project feasible, but its novelty is low. I did not open the data files.
